title: The Impact of Pollution on Worker Productivity
research_question: Does exposure to ambient ozone pollution reduce the productivity of workers engaged in physically demanding outdoor labor, even at concentrations below prevailing air-quality standards? The aim is to quantify the causal effect of daily ozone fluctuations on output per worker on the intensive margin, separate from any labor supply response.
data_description: The authors use a proprietary panel dataset from an electronic piece-rate payroll system (PET Tiger by Orange Enterprises) covering daily worker output at a single approximately 500-acre farm in California's Central Valley during the 2009 and 2010 growing seasons. The data follow roughly 1,664 workers across 155 harvest days, with worker-day observations totaling about 35,461. Variables include daily pieces harvested, hours worked, time in/out, gender, farm tenure, crop type (blueberries and two grape varietals), and contract terms (time-plus-pieces or time-plus-all-pieces with an $8 minimum wage floor). These records are merged with hourly ambient ozone, temperature, dew point, atmospheric pressure, wind speed, solar radiation, precipitation, and PM2.5 from California Air Resources Board monitoring stations within roughly 10–20 miles of the farm, averaged over the 6 a.m.–3 p.m. workday.
institutional_context: The setting is commercial fruit harvesting in California's Central Valley, where workers pick blueberries and grapes under piece-rate compensation contracts subject to a binding hourly minimum wage. Workers travel to fields in crews and remain outdoors throughout the workday, making short-run avoidance of ambient air conditions essentially infeasible. Ground-level ozone in the region is largely formed through nonlinear photochemical reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds transported from distant urban centers such as Los Angeles and San Francisco, generating substantial day-to-day variation in local ozone that is plausibly unrelated to local economic activity or worker characteristics. Because piece rates tie pay directly to output (with job retention as the marginal incentive when the minimum wage binds), output measures closely reflect productive effort. The setting also coincides with ongoing U.S. EPA deliberations over tightening the federal 8-hour ozone standard by roughly 10 ppb.
